stories.headline: India’s economy keeps humming despite Iran war
stories.title: India’s economy keeps humming despite Iran war
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
candidate gate: no category but HIGH+ priority -> allowed
article_sentences: Gross domestic product likely grew by a median 7.3%, showed an ET poll of 10 economists, with estimates ranging from 6.7% to 8%.
RBI pegged June quarter growth at 7%.
The economy grew 7.8% in the March quarter and 6.8% in Q1FY26.
The National Statistical Office (NSO) will release official GDP data for Q1 on August 31.
“High frequency indicators across the industrial and services sectors have revealed a healthy picture of domestic volume growth in Q1FY27,” said ICRA’s chief economist Aditi Nayar.
“They belie the concerns of a fallout of the West Asia conflict in the quarter,” said Nayar.

Radhika Rao, senior economist and executive director at DBS Bank, said corporate earnings indicators were also broadly constructive, with aggregate revenue growth across listed firms remaining resilient, though higher energy prices crimped profitability at oil marketing companies.
Investment activity strengthened, with the Centre’s capital expenditure rising 18.6% in Q1FY27, compared with 9.1% in the previous quarter.
“Manufacturing activity remained buoyant, supported by strong volume growth,” said Sakshi Gupta, principal economist at HDFC Bank.
“The squeeze on profit margins has been offset by the increase in volume sales.”
Nayar however said elevated input costs likely weighed on profitability across some sectors, and consequently value-added growth in the quarter, compressing GDP expansion.
Services activity remained buoyant, with the services purchasing managers’ index rising to 58.6 on average in Q1FY27 from 58 in the previous quarter.

stories.headline: Spare Jhelum’s flood plains!
stories.title: Spare Jhelum’s flood plains!
stories.summary: Why have successive regimes failed to increase the carrying capacity of river Jhelum, to mitigate flood threats? The problem lies with lack of planning, a disregard towards sustainable development! While Kashmir grapples with flood threats every time it receives incessant rains, government and people engage in blame game over destruction of river Jhelum and encroachment of its floodplains. Amid the chaos, a new proposal has surfaced up to construct a plug-and-play industrial park in Srinagar’s Nowgam area which forms part of the river’s flood plains. Nowgam Industrial Park will spread across 50 acres with a projected investment of Rs 104.02 crore. The project will be executed under the Bharat Audyogik Vikas Yojana (BHAVYA), a flagship Central scheme aimed at developing next-generation Plug-and-Play Industrial Parks. The Nowgam project will focus on the horticulture value chain, food processing, warehousing, light manufacturing and digital services. A welcome development indeed as it will generate employment avenues and prove boon for the horticulture sector. But authorities must conduct an Environmental Impact Assessment of the project site and determine the impact of the project in case Jhelum swells during floods. We have to understand the topography of Jhelum and the role of its floodplains. Jhelum, considered to be Kashmir’s lifeline, spans 175 sq kms from south to north Kashmir. Jhelum meanders in a serpentine way from south to north Kashmir and settles in Wullar, Asia’s largest freshwater lake, before pouring into other side of Kashmir, across the Line of Control through the Uri area of north Kashmir’s Baramulla district. The five upstream watersheds of Upper Jhelum Basin—Lidder, Kuthar, Bringi, Sandran, and Vishav, all drain into the river. The right bank tributaries of Jhelum are Lidder and Kuthar, which originate in the Greater Himalayan Range. The left bank tributaries are the Bringi, Sandran, and Vishav, which originate in the Pir Panjal Range. The problem starts when Jhelum water from south Kashmir reaches Srinagar. The river’s topography makes Srinagar the most vulnerable area to flooding in J&K. Wetlands on the left and right of Jhelum in Srinagar act as reservoirs of the floodwaters. Ecologically important wetlands in the Jhelum floodplains like Hokersar, Bemina wetland, Narakara wetland, Batamaloo nambal, Rakh-e-arth, Anchar lake and Gilsar reduce pressure of Jhelum during floods. Vast chunks of open land from Shalina, Kandizal, Lasjan and Nowgam act as Jhelum’s floodplains. Ironically in absence of regulation by authorities, wetlands in Srinagar and even the floodplains have been extensively encroached upon, filled up and dotted with constructions. Flood events over the decades have shown how geomorphic, climatic, and socio-economic settings have exacerbated its flood risk especially in Srinagar. The problem has been compounded by weak flood control infrastructure, shrinking wetlands, deforestation, massive urbanisation of floodplains, and siltation, filling of Jhelum’s watercourses. Earth filling and construction has swallowed wetlands and floodplains at Nowgam, Lasjan, Mehjoor Nagar, Bemina, Hokersar, Zainakote, Narbal, Soibugh, Hyderpora and Pir Bagh. The construction of Bypass through Gallander and Pampore, together with the Srinagar Semi Ring Road project and Railway Track hamper flow of Jhelum water during floods. During the recent floods on September 4 last year, Jhelum flowed through its erstwhile encroached floodplains from Shalina to Lasjan areas, Soiteng, Nowgam, Vyethpora, Gopalpora, Padshibagh, Mehjoor Nagar. People of these areas were shifted to safer places amid breach at Shalina-Jhelum embankment. It was a practice of Dogra rulers to breach the Kandzal area to save Srinagar from floods. Excess water of Jhelum used to be diverted through the Kandzal area and the waters would spread to Nowgam areas. However, there have been massive constructions not only in Kandzal areas but adjoining flood plains spreading upto Nowgam. The built-up area within the floodplains of Jhelum has increased by four times from 55.47 sq. km in 1972 to over 200 sq. km. It is shocking that the Irrigation and Flood Control Department has not undertaken dredging in Jhelum and other flood channels for the period from March 2020 to March 2025. It is claimed that since devastating floods in September 2014, the carrying capacity of Jhelum has been increased from 30800 cusecs to 41000 cusecs. As per experts, there is a shortfall of 60000 cusecs as 2014 floods generated over 1 lakh cusecs of water submerging habitations around the river. The National Green Tribunal had last year stalled construction of an industrial estate in Trenz village, South Kashmir’s Shopian district, citing serious environmental and flood-related concerns, following a petition filed by environmental activist Dr. Raja Muzaffar Bhat. The petitioner stated that the project site, covering approximately 500 kanals of government land, falls within the natural floodplain of the Rambiara River and poses a severe threat to downstream communities, agricultural lands, and apple orchards. This project site is within the natural floodway of the river. Kashmir valley is one of the most flood hazard-prone regions in the Himalayas. The valley has been witnessing frequent floods for centuries. It witnessed floods on regular intervals with major ones in 1903, 1905, 1909, 1928, 1948, 1950, 1951, 1953, 1954, 1956, 1957, 1959, 1962, 1963, 1964, 1969, 1972, 1973, 1976, 1986, 1992, 1995, 1996, 2006 and the devastating one in 2014. Experts maintain that floods are mostly caused by the filling up of Jhelum’s flood plains and backwater effects due to low outflows from Wullar Lake which over the decades has lost its carrying capacity by heavy accumulation of silt. Government must on priority increase the carrying capacity of Jhelum. Given the climatic changes and erratic weather pattern in J&K, the Government must ensure to go for sustainable development. Loss of 31 human lives and massive destruction of property by recent spree of flash floods triggered by incessant rains and cloudbursts in J&K must serve as eye-opener. We can’t afford to disturb and damage nature more and must for sustainable development and conduct Environmental Impact Assessment before executiveny any project in eco-fragile areas. We need to understand that development can’t be done at the cost of the environment! Author is Executive Editor, Greater Kashmir

stories.headline: LoC villages await bunkers despite shelling threat
stories.title: LoC villages await bunkers despite shelling threat
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 16: More than a year after Operation Sindoor, residents living along the Line of Control (LoC) in Uri sector of north Kashmir’s Baramulla district say they continue to live under the threat of cross-border shelling, with no new community bunkers visible on the ground. Residents said that despite repeated demands for safe shelters, the construction of new bunkers has not progressed in several border villages. They also claimed that many of the existing bunkers have either deteriorated or are no longer fit to provide adequate protection during shelling. Lal Hussain Kohli, a resident of Charunda village along the LoC, told Rising Kashmir that no new bunker has been constructed in the area since Operation Sindoor. “Not a single new bunker has been built by the government in the last one year. Whatever bunkers we have were constructed nearly five years ago,” he said. Kohli said the village remains vulnerable to cross-border firing and requires functional shelters for the protection of civilians. “There are around eight community bunkers here, but all of them are in a dilapidated condition and cannot be used safely,” he said. Similar concerns were raised by residents of other border villages, including Garkote, Mothal and Silikote. Bashir Ahmad Bhat of Garkote said villagers had received no government support for bunker construction after Operation Sindoor. “If cross-border shelling happens again, where are we supposed to go?” he asked, adding that some families had been forced to construct makeshift shelters using their own limited resources. “We are poor people, but we have no choice. We have to protect our families,” Bhat said. Nadeem Abbasi, an ex-sarpanch of Gawalta village along LoC said that no new bunker had been constructed in the village and residents continued to face serious risks during any escalation along the LoC. “No new bunker has come up here. Our lives continue to remain at risk,” Abbasi said, adding that several older bunkers had also deteriorated and could no longer safely accommodate residents during shelling. The issue of civilian shelters in Uri has remained a concern for years. In 2020, the government had proposed the construction of several community bunkers in the border area. While some were completed, residents said many remained unfinished or inadequate. In May last year, the then Deputy Commissioner, Baramulla, approved the construction of 202 overhead protection trenches in the Uri sector. However, some residents questioned their effectiveness and termed them a waste of public money. “They dug shallow trenches and covered them with wooden planks and mud. Such structures are unsafe during heavy shelling. We need proper concrete bunkers,” said Tariq Hashim, a resident of Kamalkote sector. The issue gained further attention in January this year when then Deputy Commissioner Baramulla Minga Sherpa said that the Home Department had sanctioned more than 500 bunkers to be constructed along the LoC in Uri. However, residents said there was little visible progress on the ground and urged the administration to expedite the construction of durable and fully equipped shelters before any fresh escalation along the LoC. When contacted, Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM) Uri Prince Kumar said the matter had already been taken up with the higher authorities. “A proposal in this regard has already been sent to the government,” he told Rising Kashmir.

stories.headline: Reviving the Willow
stories.title: Reviving the Willow
stories.summary: The Government of Jammu and Kashmir’s recent engagement with the willow-based cricket-bat industry is a welcome and timely beginning. On 29th July 2026, the Chief Minister Omar Abdullah’s interaction with manufacturers at Sangam, his assurance of a steady supply of quality willow, acknowledges a fundamental reality: the future of Kashmir’s cricket-bat industry cannot be separated from the future of the tree on which it depends. What is now required is a sustained, scientifically designed mission that treats willow cultivation, bat manufacturing, environmental stewardship, industrial infrastructure, research, employment and marketing as parts of a single economic ecosystem, rather than as separate problems to be handled department by department. Willow was once inseparable from Kashmir’s landscape, lining roadsides, marking agricultural boundaries and flourishing near water bodies across the Valley. In my own village, Veeri, a popular belief connects the settlement’s name to the Kashmiri word for willow, “Veer” – an etymology open to scholarly scrutiny, but revealing of how deeply the tree was embedded in local memory and rural life. That presence has gradually diminished even as the industry built around it has grown into one of national and international standing, exporting a distinctly Kashmiri product to cricket-playing nations around the world. Kashmir today has close to 400 cricket-bat manufacturing units, concentrated mainly in the Sangam-Awantipora belt. The sector produces an estimated 1.5 million bats a year, generates an annual turnover of nearly Rs 300 crore, and directly or indirectly sustains more than a lakh livelihoods. This is no small cottage enterprise; it is a substantial economic chain connecting farmers, willow growers, timber suppliers, artisans, manufacturers, traders and transporters. Any disruption in the availability of quality willow therefore ripples through this entire network, from the grower’s field to the export consignment. The scale of this network means that raw-material shortages are never simply a manufacturing-floor problem. When quality willow becomes scarce or expensive, smaller units are the first to suffer, since they lack the reserves to stockpile timber or absorb rising costs, while larger manufacturers face pressure on margins that ultimately affects wages and expansion plans. A shortage today therefore shapes the industry’s competitiveness for years to come. Why the willow is running out Today’s shortage of raw material has built up over years, driven mainly by two factors. First, many cultivators replaced willow with Russian poplar or converted their land to apple orchards, both of which offered quicker or more sustained financial returns. These were entirely rational choices for individual farmers weighing their own income, but their cumulative effect across the Valley was a steep decline in land under high-quality willow suitable for bat manufacturing. Second, productive land, including willow-bearing land, has been steadily acquired for government institutions and industrial estates, particularly in Anantnag district after 2019. This trend must be weighed against the record of estates already established there: the Anantnag Industrial Area (1960), Bijbehara Industrial Estate (1962), the Sports Goods Complex under SICOP (1978), Anachidora Industrial Estate (1982) and Vessu Industrial Estate (2006). Despite decades in existence, many of these have still not achieved the industrial potential envisaged at their founding. Before further land is committed to new estates, the Government would do well to rigorously assess the utilisation, employment generation and future viability of the ones that already exist, rather than repeating the same pattern on fresh ground. This question matters more in Kashmir than in most other regions because of its geography: a limited landmass of roughly 90 by 45 miles, difficult terrain, and weather that frequently disrupts connectivity with the rest of the country, raising transport costs and weakening supply chains for any industry dependent on the uninterrupted movement of goods. Under these constraints, agriculture and agriculture-linked enterprise remain among Kashmir’s strongest economic assets, and the willow-cricket bat sector, rooted in local ecology, traditional skill and a globally recognised sporting product, is an outstanding example of that natural advantage. Policies that erode the land base underlying this relationship risk undermining, perhaps unintentionally, an industry in which Kashmir holds a genuine comparative advantage over any other producing region. Willow Revival Mission Building on its recent engagement with manufacturers, the Government should launch a comprehensive Willow Revival Mission bringing together the Departments of Forest, Environment, Agriculture, Industries and Commerce, Horticulture, Social Forestry and Sports, along with farmers, manufacturers, scientific institutions, financial agencies and local representatives. The mission should begin with a scientific inventory of existing willow resources – their location, age, species, quality, ownership and expected harvesting period – so that the industry is not compelled to confront a raw-material crisis every few years for want of reliable, long-term data. Farmers should then be encouraged to grow suitable willow varieties on private and other identified, ecologically appropriate land, supported by quality saplings, technical guidance, access to credit, insurance and assured market linkages, so that growers can be confident their investment will yield remunerative returns. In parallel, agricultural and forestry institutions should study which varieties suit Kashmir’s changing climate, and the growth rates, disease resistance and physical properties needed to produce durable, high-performing bats. Ecological considerations must remain central to this programme. Wetlands, including Wular Lake, are essential to Kashmir’s environmental security, and willow expansion should never come at their cost. There is, however, considerable scope for scientific plantation on suitable revenue land, degraded areas and agricultural boundaries without disturbing fragile ecosystems. The Marhama Nambal area, for instance, could be reclaimed – its blocked drainage restored for an estimated Rs 50 lakh to Rs 1 crore – and, as the Chief Minister has himself suggested, divided into scientifically planned compartments for water-intensive willow cultivation. The Rakh-i-Momin tract near Hafizabad, Loktipora and Arwani offers another substantial opportunity, potentially developed with the Social Forestry Department, as do suitable areas in Ajas, Bandipora and around Wular, subject to environmental safeguards and scientific assessment. The aim should not be simply to plant more trees, but to plant the right varieties in the right places, maintained scientifically and harvested on a predictable cycle, so that quality and long-term supply, not sheer numbers, guide the programme. Sethar and Bijbehara Two existing public assets illustrate both the industry’s unrealised potential and the cost of institutional delay. The Common Facility Centre at Sethar was established in 2005 under the Centre’s Cluster Development Programme, with roughly 14 kanals of state land and Rs 246.46 lakh worth of Centrally funded machinery, including 25 seasoning chambers, 10 boilers and a solar seasoning unit. It was meant to give manufacturers common access to modern processing technology and improve the quality and uniformity of Kashmir willow bats, but the 2014 floods left it largely non-functional. Renovation was subsequently taken up under the World Bank-funded Jhelum Tawi Flood Recovery Project, which also saw the belt from Jawbehara-Awantipora to Doonipora-Sangam along NH-44 declared an industrial zone for cricket-bat manufacturing. Of an estimated project cost of Rs 461 lakh, Rs 451.95 lakh was released, yet essential work -- insulation, flooring and tracks for moving willow clefts -- remains unfinished. The World Bank’s subsequent withdrawal from the project, and the diversion of about Rs 4 crore earmarked for the facility to pandemic-response spending, has left an institution built for one of Kashmir’s most important traditional industries still short of operational. It should now be completed without further delay, modernised with vacuum-based seasoning chambers, quality-control laboratories and reliable power infrastructure, and equipped to offer training, product development and marketing support, particularly to smaller manufacturers. The Sports Goods Complex at Jablipora, Bijbehara, tells a similar story. Built on roughly 206 kanals acquired in 1976-77 at the initiative of Sher-i-Kashmir Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah and the then MLA, Abdul Gani Veeri, and transferred to JKSICOP in 1979, it originally allotted 64 kanals to 49 manufacturing units. Militancy in the 1990s disrupted its development; most structures came under security-forces occupation, only two of the original units remain functional, and roughly 48 kanals are now under mulberry cultivation. A 2019 attempt to allot vacant land to new entrepreneurs – 27 kanals were earmarked for 12 applicants out of 25 who applied – made only limited headway, and in 2020 the estate was renamed Industrial Estate Bijbehara, with its scope widened to agriculture and horticulture alongside sports goods. The Government should now examine restoring it to its original purpose, resolving occupancy issues, and upgrading it to house common processing facilities, testing laboratories, and training and incubation space for new entrepreneurs -- reviving an existing public investment rather than acquiring fresh agricultural land for industrial use. Science, certification and the global market Long-term competitiveness will depend on science as much as on supply. A dedicated Willow and Cricket-Bat Research and Development Centre, developed with SKUAST-K and other scientific institutions, could study the growth, density, strength, moisture behaviour and playing performance of Kashmir willow, and help manufacturers adopt modern technology without eroding the traditional craftsmanship that gives their bats a distinctive character. A credible certification and traceability system -- standardised grading, quality certification and geographical indication -- would let buyers distinguish genuine Kashmir willow from inferior or mislabelled alternatives, strengthening both consumer confidence and the industry’s position in export markets. Willow was once inseparable from Kashmir’s landscape, lining roadsides, marking agricultural boundaries and flourishing near water bodies across the Valley.

In my own village, Veeri, a popular belief connects the settlement’s name to the Kashmiri word for willow, “Veer” – an etymology open to scholarly scrutiny, but revealing of how deeply the tree was embedded in local memory and rural life.

That presence has gradually diminished even as the industry built around it has grown into one of national and international standing, exporting a distinctly Kashmiri product to cricket-playing nations around the world.
Kashmir today has close to 400 cricket-bat manufacturing units, concentrated mainly in the Sangam-Awantipora belt.
The sector produces an estimated 1.5 million bats a year, generates an annual turnover of nearly Rs 300 crore, and directly or indirectly sustains more than a lakh livelihoods.
This is no small cottage enterprise; it is a substantial economic chain connecting farmers, willow growers, timber suppliers, artisans, manufacturers, traders and transporters.
Any disruption in the availability of quality willow therefore ripples through this entire network, from the grower’s field to the export consignment.
The scale of this network means that raw-material shortages are never simply a manufacturing-floor problem.

When quality willow becomes scarce or expensive, smaller units are the first to suffer, since they lack the reserves to stockpile timber or absorb rising costs, while larger manufacturers face pressure on margins that ultimately affects wages and expansion plans.
A shortage today therefore shapes the industry’s competitiveness for years to come.
Why the willow is running out Today’s shortage of raw material has built up over years, driven mainly by two factors.
First, many cultivators replaced willow with Russian poplar or converted their land to apple orchards, both of which offered quicker or more sustained financial returns.

These were entirely rational choices for individual farmers weighing their own income, but their cumulative effect across the Valley was a steep decline in land under high-quality willow suitable for bat manufacturing.
Second, productive land, including willow-bearing land, has been steadily acquired for government institutions and industrial estates, particularly in Anantnag district after 2019.

This trend must be weighed against the record of estates already established there: the Anantnag Industrial Area (1960), Bijbehara Industrial Estate (1962), the Sports Goods Complex under SICOP (1978), Anachidora Industrial Estate (1982) and Vessu Industrial Estate (2006).
Despite decades in existence, many of these have still not achieved the industrial potential envisaged at their founding.

Before further land is committed to new estates, the Government would do well to rigorously assess the utilisation, employment generation and future viability of the ones that already exist, rather than repeating the same pattern on fresh ground.

This question matters more in Kashmir than in most other regions because of its geography: a limited landmass of roughly 90 by 45 miles, difficult terrain, and weather that frequently disrupts connectivity with the rest of the country, raising transport costs and weakening supply chains for any industry dependent on the uninterrupted movement of goods.

Under these constraints, agriculture and agriculture-linked enterprise remain among Kashmir’s strongest economic assets, and the willow-cricket bat sector, rooted in local ecology, traditional skill and a globally recognised sporting product, is an outstanding example of that natural advantage.

Policies that erode the land base underlying this relationship risk undermining, perhaps unintentionally, an industry in which Kashmir holds a genuine comparative advantage over any other producing region.

Willow Revival Mission Building on its recent engagement with manufacturers, the Government should launch a comprehensive Willow Revival Mission bringing together the Departments of Forest, Environment, Agriculture, Industries and Commerce, Horticulture, Social Forestry and Sports, along with farmers, manufacturers, scientific institutions, financial agencies and local representatives.

The mission should begin with a scientific inventory of existing willow resources – their location, age, species, quality, ownership and expected harvesting period – so that the industry is not compelled to confront a raw-material crisis every few years for want of reliable, long-term data.

Farmers should then be encouraged to grow suitable willow varieties on private and other identified, ecologically appropriate land, supported by quality saplings, technical guidance, access to credit, insurance and assured market linkages, so that growers can be confident their investment will yield remunerative returns.

In parallel, agricultural and forestry institutions should study which varieties suit Kashmir’s changing climate, and the growth rates, disease resistance and physical properties needed to produce durable, high-performing bats.
Ecological considerations must remain central to this programme.
Wetlands, including Wular Lake, are essential to Kashmir’s environmental security, and willow expansion should never come at their cost.
There is, however, considerable scope for scientific plantation on suitable revenue land, degraded areas and agricultural boundaries without disturbing fragile ecosystems.

The Marhama Nambal area, for instance, could be reclaimed – its blocked drainage restored for an estimated Rs 50 lakh to Rs 1 crore – and, as the Chief Minister has himself suggested, divided into scientifically planned compartments for water-intensive willow cultivation.

The Rakh-i-Momin tract near Hafizabad, Loktipora and Arwani offers another substantial opportunity, potentially developed with the Social Forestry Department, as do suitable areas in Ajas, Bandipora and around Wular, subject to environmental safeguards and scientific assessment.

The aim should not be simply to plant more trees, but to plant the right varieties in the right places, maintained scientifically and harvested on a predictable cycle, so that quality and long-term supply, not sheer numbers, guide the programme.
Sethar and Bijbehara.
Two existing public assets illustrate both the industry’s unrealised potential and the cost of institutional delay.

The Common Facility Centre at Sethar was established in 2005 under the Centre’s Cluster Development Programme, with roughly 14 kanals of state land and Rs 246.46 lakh worth of Centrally funded machinery, including 25 seasoning chambers, 10 boilers and a solar seasoning unit.
It was meant to give manufacturers common access to modern processing technology and improve the quality and uniformity of Kashmir willow bats, but the 2014 floods left it largely non-functional.

Renovation was subsequently taken up under the World Bank-funded Jhelum Tawi Flood Recovery Project, which also saw the belt from Jawbehara-Awantipora to Doonipora-Sangam along NH-44 declared an industrial zone for cricket-bat manufacturing.
Of an estimated project cost of Rs 461 lakh, Rs 451.95 lakh was released, yet essential work -- insulation, flooring and tracks for moving willow clefts -- remains unfinished.

The World Bank’s subsequent withdrawal from the project, and the diversion of about Rs 4 crore earmarked for the facility to pandemic-response spending, has left an institution built for one of Kashmir’s most important traditional industries still short of operational.

It should now be completed without further delay, modernised with vacuum-based seasoning chambers, quality-control laboratories and reliable power infrastructure, and equipped to offer training, product development and marketing support, particularly to smaller manufacturers.
The Sports Goods Complex at Jablipora, Bijbehara, tells a similar story.

Built on roughly 206 kanals acquired in 1976-77 at the initiative of Sher-i-Kashmir Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah and the then MLA, Abdul Gani Veeri, and transferred to JKSICOP in 1979, it originally allotted 64 kanals to 49 manufacturing units.

Militancy in the 1990s disrupted its development; most structures came under security-forces occupation, only two of the original units remain functional, and roughly 48 kanals are now under mulberry cultivation.

A 2019 attempt to allot vacant land to new entrepreneurs – 27 kanals were earmarked for 12 applicants out of 25 who applied – made only limited headway, and in 2020 the estate was renamed Industrial Estate Bijbehara, with its scope widened to agriculture and horticulture alongside sports goods.

stories.headline: Israel intensifies strikes on Southern Lebanon killing 11 as Iran-Oman talks continue over Strait of Hormuz
stories.title: Israel intensifies strikes on Southern Lebanon killing 11 as Iran-Oman talks continue over Strait of Hormuz
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 16: Israel has intensified its military operations in southern Lebanon, killing at least 11 people in what Al Jazeera described as the deadliest attacks since a US-brokered ceasefire framework was agreed in June, while tensions between Iran and the United States remain high over the Strait of Hormuz and the future of negotiations. Israeli forces continued to bombard southern Lebanon on Saturday, with explosions reported near Ali al-Taher Heights following a series of attacks that left at least 11 people dead. In an overnight Israeli strike hit a family home in Ansar in southern Lebanon, killing at least seven people, including children, according to Al Jazeera. The latest attacks have raised fresh concerns about the durability of the US-brokered ceasefire framework reached between Israel and Lebanon in June. Lebanese and Iranian authorities have condemned the strikes, while the Arab League described the escalation as a serious threat to efforts to resolve the conflict. An Arab League spokesperson said the attacks could undermine attempts to end the fighting and accused Israel of seeking to prolong the confrontation and impose a new reality on the ground. The Arab League also called on the international community, particularly Washington, to restrain Israel and ensure compliance with UN Security Council Resolution 1701. Adopted in 2006, the resolution calls for an end to hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah and requires the cessation of attacks by Hezbollah and offensive military operations by Israel. The US State Department, however, told Al Jazeera that Hezbollah bears responsibility for the continued presence of Israeli forces on Lebanese territory. The US official described Hezbollah as the principal obstacle to Lebanon's economic recovery and said a proposed “pilot zone” arrangement remained the most viable route towards peace. Under the arrangement, Israeli forces would withdraw from certain areas while Lebanese troops would move into them. The latest violence comes amid continuing uncertainty over whether the June ceasefire framework can hold as Israel maintains military positions and carries out strikes in parts of southern Lebanon. The escalation also comes against a wider regional backdrop, with Yemen's Houthis launching another ballistic missile towards the government-held city of Marib, according to local officials, while Syrian civil defence teams dealt with a fire reportedly caused by Israeli forces firing flares in the town of al-Rafid. Meanwhile, Hamas political bureau chief Khalil al-Hayya is expected to travel to Cairo for talks aimed at consolidating the Gaza ceasefire. Iran-US standoff deepens as Tehran links Hormuz reopening to US actions On the Iran-US front, the immediate focus remains on the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz, where Tehran says it is continuing discussions with Oman on possible new shipping routes. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran and Muscat could reach an agreement soon on a new route through the waterway. But he stressed that reaching an agreement on shipping routes and reopening the Strait of Hormuz were “two separate issues”, according to Al Jazeera. Araghchi said reopening the waterway would depend on Washington fulfilling conditions under a memorandum of understanding signed in June. Among Tehran's demands are an end to US sanctions and the release of Iranian assets, he said. “Iran’s foreign minister said that Tehran and Oman ‘may reach an outcome soon’ on a new route in the Strait of Hormuz,” Al Jazeera reported. However, Araghchi made clear that any decision to reopen the waterway would depend on the fulfilment of wider conditions by the United States. The comments underline the distance that remains between Tehran and Washington despite diplomatic messages being exchanged through intermediaries. Araghchi said on Friday that no decision had been taken on returning to direct talks with the United States. Qatar and Pakistan, meanwhile, have been exchanging messages between the two sides in an effort to keep diplomatic channels open. The standoff has been further complicated by US President Donald Trump's comments on the Strait of Hormuz. Trump has said that after what he described as defeating Iran, he would declare the strategic waterway US territory. Tehran responded sharply, saying on X that the Strait of Hormuz “has been Iranian, is Iranian, and will remain Iranian”. US officials, meanwhile, have indicated that Washington could maintain its naval blockade of Iranian ports indefinitely and impose additional economic measures on Tehran. The Trump administration has increasingly signalled that it would prefer economic pressure to launching another major military offensive. For Iran, however, the reopening of the Strait remains tied to broader political and economic demands. The waterway is crucial to global energy supplies, making the dispute over its status and shipping routes a major international concern. The developments also highlight the fragile nature of the wider regional situation. While diplomatic efforts involving Oman and other intermediaries continue, the continuing violence in Lebanon and the unresolved confrontation between Iran and the US leave the region facing the risk of another escalation.

stories.headline: CS orders faster rollout of MHA-approved Rs 1579-Cr disaster package
stories.title: CS orders faster rollout of MHA-approved Rs 1579-Cr disaster package
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 16: Chief Secretary Atal Dulloo on Sunday reviewed the implementation of the Recovery and Reconstruction (R&R) Plan-2025 and utilisation of the disaster recovery assistance sanctioned for Jammu and Kashmir by the Centre directing departments to accelerate project formulation and execution while ensuring that every reconstructed asset is made more resilient to future disasters. The Chief Secretary took detailed stock of the Rs 1579.09 crore recovery package approved by the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) under the NDRF and SDRF R&R Funding Window. The same was approved through MHA for Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA) for damages caused by floods, cloudbursts, landslides and other disasters to the tune of Rs 1534.58 crore, besides Rs 44.52 crore for the dedicated Ramban District recovery plan following the April 2025 cloudburst and flash floods. Reviewing the progress, the Chief Secretary noted that departments have so far prepared costed action plans amounting to Rs 1225.78 crore, leaving a balance of Rs 353.31 crore to be operationalised by the Jal Shakti and Agriculture sectors. Emphasising that disaster recovery should not merely restore damaged infrastructure to its pre-disaster condition, the Chief Secretary directed all executing agencies to strictly follow the ‘Build Back Better’ (BBB) approach. Dulloo also called for strict cross-verification of beneficiary lists and project proposals with major ongoing schemes, including PMAY-G, JalJeevan Mission, AMRUT, SASCI, NABARD, PMGSY and Samagra Shiksha, to eliminate any possibility of duplication and ensure optimal use of public resources. He called for reconstructed assets to incorporate appropriate disaster-resilient features, including compliance with Seismic Zone IV/V requirements, elevated plinths and slope stabilization measures, wherever applicable. The departments were also asked to optimally utilise both norm-based and flexible assistance available under the approved recovery framework to meet incremental resilience requirements. The Chief Secretary further directed that all projects be geo-tagged forthwith and uploaded on the BEAMS digital platform, creating a unified digital record for monitoring progress, financial utilization and physical outcomes. Giving the sector-wise review, the Principal Secretary, DMRR&R, Chandraker Bharti revealed that significant progress has been achieved in several components of the recovery programme. In the social sector, he highlighted against an approved allocation of Rs 289.40 crore, departments have formulated plans amounting to Rs 262.11 crore. Similarly in the Housing component 100 percent commitment of its Rs 193.19 crore allocation, covering 9083 households, including 5227 fully and 3856 severely damaged houses has been achieved. With respect to the Roads and Bridges component, it has emerged as one of the strongest performing infrastructure segments, with its entire Rs 461.64 crore allocation planned for restoration of approximately 1230.7 km of roads and 4494.5 metres of bridges. Additionally, the power sector has planned utilisation of Rs 70.08 crore against Rs 72.97 crore, targeting restoration of more than 21,000 poles, 1100 circuit kilometres of conductors and 800 transformers, benefiting around 1.45 lakh consumers. The meeting was apprised that the drinking water and sanitation has so far formulated plans for Rs 59.02 crore against Rs 139.65 crore, while Irrigation and Flood Control has planned Rs 93.01 crore against Rs 199.79 crore and are in a process of utilising the full kitty of funds available. In the productive sectors, agriculture has formulated plans worth Rs 168.36 crore against Rs 223.67 crore, covering 45 packages relating to crop inputs, land reclamation and restoration of research infrastructure at SKUAST-Jammu. Animal husbandry and livestock has planned Rs 8.86 crore against Rs 10.28 crore, while horticulture has fully utilised its Rs 3.87 crore allocation to support 3493 farmers. The Chief Secretary also reviewed the dedicated Rs 44.52 croreRamban recovery plan prepared in response to the cloudburst and flash floods of April 19-20, 2025. The plan includes Rs 23.24 crore for roads and bridges, Rs 3.34 crore for irrigation and flood control, Rs 1.78 crore for education and Rs 1.48 crore for animal husbandry and livestock, with approved and proposed allocations fully reconciled in these components. The Chief Secretary directed that household relief under the recovery programme be disbursed strictly in accordance with the 30:40:30 progress-linked Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) pattern, ensuring that payments remain aligned with actual progress of reconstruction. He directed block, sub-divisional, and district-level nodal officers to ensure complete resolution of E-Samadhan and CPGRAMS grievances within 15 days, making grievance redressal an integral part of the recovery monitoring mechanism. The Chief Secretary underscored that the recovery programme should result not only in timely restoration of damaged assets but also in a more resilient and disaster-ready J&K, with every rupee sanctioned translating into durable public infrastructure and tangible relief for affected communities. The meeting was attended by Additional Chief Secretary, Finance; Additional Chief Secretary, PWD; Principal Secretary, DMRR&R; Director, CD and SDRF; Administrative Secretaries, Divisional Commissioner, Jammu/Kashmir; and other senior officers. Deputy Commissioners from all 20 districts participated virtually.

The Chief Secretary underscored that the recovery programme should result not only in timely restoration of damaged assets but also in a more resilient and disaster-ready J&K, with every rupee sanctioned translating into durable public infrastructure and tangible relief for affected communities.

The meeting was attended by Additional Chief Secretary, Finance; Additional Chief Secretary, PWD; Principal Secretary, DMRR&R; Director, CD and SDRF; Administrative Secretaries, Divisional Commissioner, Jammu/Kashmir; and other senior officers.
Deputy Commissioners from all 20 districts participated virtually.

sentences.text: Srinagar, Aug 16: Chief Secretary Atal Dulloo on Sunday reviewed the implementation of the Recovery and Reconstruction (R&R) Plan-2025 and utilisation of the disaster recovery assistance sanctioned for Jammu and Kashmir by the Centre directing departments to accelerate project formulation and execution while ensuring that every reconstructed asset is made more resilient to future disasters.

The same was approved through MHA for Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA) for damages caused by floods, cloudbursts, landslides and other disasters to the tune of Rs 1534.58 crore, besides Rs 44.52 crore for the dedicated Ramban District recovery plan following the April 2025 cloudburst and flash floods.

In the productive sectors, agriculture has formulated plans worth Rs 168.36 crore against Rs 223.67 crore, covering 45 packages relating to crop inputs, land reclamation and restoration of research infrastructure at SKUAST-Jammu.
The Chief Secretary also reviewed the dedicated Rs 44.52 croreRamban recovery plan prepared in response to the cloudburst and flash floods of April 19-20, 2025.

stories.headline: Banks may rush to tap short loans abroad
stories.title: Banks may rush to tap short loans abroad
stories.summary: MUMBAI: Friday's central bank move to shorten the swap-support window for overseas deposits will likely prompt banks to raise short-term loans abroad and quicken deposit collection as regulatory latitude on the foreign currency non-resident-bank (FCNR-B) programme ends in less than two weeks, people aware of the developments said. Overall foreign borrowings by banks, however, will likely be lower than earlier estimates.Bankers said some lenders now plan to borrow more short-term funds, possibly at a higher rate, to finance the promised leverage to FCNR(B) clients after the Reserve Bank of India advanced the deadline for swap support. These funds will have to be replaced with a long-term loan or bond later, leading to a temporary mismatch between banks' foreign deposits and borrowings."The RBI has put banks in a tight spot. Banks had done roadshows, spent manhours on getting documentation ready and put a lot of investments into this. All this was planned with September 30 deadline in mind," said a senior private-sector bank executive.Since large funds can't be secured for a longer tenure immediately, one option is to look for bridge loans."Not many banks have the capacity to raise a huge sum at such a short notice; so one option banks are exploring is to do a short-term bridge loan for now to ensure customers can be provided leverage on their deposits until the end of August. These short-term loans can be replaced with longer term borrowings later," said the executive cited above.'Sufficient'On Friday, the RBI advanced the deadline for mobilising FCNR-B deposits to August 31, from the originally announced September 30, citing higher-than-expected inflows. The RBI received $52.3 billion through FCNR(B) deposits until August 13, the latest update showed.133281793Banks can use the RBI's special zero cost swap facility, until September 11, 2026, versus the earlier date of October 16.Bankers said the early closure was surprising since governor Sanjay Malhotra himself had said a week ago that the central bank neither planned to prematurely close the swap window because of robust inflows nor had it received any proposal to extend the timeline beyond the announced deadline."As of now, there is no proposal under consideration to close the scheme prematurely," Malhotra had said after the monetary policy announcement on August 5. The scheme's curtailment could expose lenders to liquidity mismatches.Late Entrants"Some banks that were late in garnering dollars will probably stop in their tracks. Others may choose not to push for more dollars, while some with customer commitments will look for short-term funds immediately - possibly at a higher cost," said another private-sector banker. "This will create mismatches in the short term, which is not healthy."For instance, ICICI Bank's $1.45 billion, four-year loan launched last week is currently under syndication. This loan also has a greenshoe option allowing ICICI Bank to upsize the total amount it wants to raise. The bank may want to wrap up the syndication early and not look at pushing the greenshoe.Similarly, Punjab National Bank's $1 billion loan, which went into syndication in the last week of July, could be closed early as the bank scampers to get funds within the shorter deadline."Some mid-to small-sized banks, which had planned debut bond sales overseas, may now have to look at alternative sources. They will have to curtail their FCNR (B) targets because it does not look like the RBI needs more dollars," said a senior executive with a foreign bank.Bankers said the RBI's decision has exposed them to risks of higher payouts immediately. There is also no certainty that whenever they tap the overseas markets, to match their three- to five-year FCNR(B) deposit liabilities, the US treasury, global rates or geopolitics will be favourable."Until last week, the RBI was in touch with banks pushing for more dollars. If dollar flows were too heavy, then there are ways to use them. Just open a special window for oil companies, for instance," said a third private sector bank executive.Bankers said by closing the scheme early and at a short notice, the RBI would be indicating it has enough muscle to protect the rupee.

The RBI received $52.3 billion through FCNR(B) deposits until August 13, the latest update showed.
Banks can use the RBI's special zero cost swap facility, until September 11, 2026, versus the earlier date of October 16.

If dollar flows were too heavy, then there are ways to use them.
Just open a special window for oil companies, for instance," said a third private sector bank executive.
Bankers said by closing the scheme early and at a short notice, the RBI would be indicating it has enough muscle to protect the rupee.
